articles.title: Your Most Important Summer Reading Isn’t On Your Syllabus
articles.content:
如果你今年秋季开始读法学院，可能已经有人告诉你该读什么。
案例书。可能还有一本合同法入门读物。帮你在第一次冷叫之前了解律师思维方式的书。
这些建议没错。
但不够全面。
因为你今年最重要的暑期阅读不在课程大纲上——那些能让你作为未来律师被看见和理解的一切。
这看起来可能与坚持"唯才是举"的法律界格格不入。但现实并非如此。

当你毕业时，LinkedIn、TikTok等平台将真正影响雇主、客户甚至同事如何接触你的想法。而ChatGPT等工具已经在改变法律信息如何被总结、呈现和信任的方式。

你不仅是在准备从事法律工作。
你是在准备如何被理解。

多数法学院学生却等太久才考虑这些。
他们理所当然地专注于成绩、期刊和实习。这些很重要，但不是全部。如今脱颖而出的学生不仅学业优秀，更是那些早早建立个人观点并让其可见的人。

这并不意味着要变成内容机器。而是要让你自己清晰可见。
别人能理解你对法律的兴趣所在吗？能看出你如何思考问题吗？当别人寻找你感兴趣的领域见解时，能找到你吗？
这些不是虚荣问题。而是专业问题。

最简单的开始方式也是最不舒服的——写点东西。不是课堂作业，不是为了成绩。而是为自己，为愿意阅读的人。
挑选你关注的案例，用通俗语言解释它。就某个真正吸引你的法律发展发表看法。公开提出你仍在寻找答案的问题。
坚持这样做，哪怕是小举动，会发生关键变化。
你不再像法学生。
开始像律师。

还有一个容易忽视的好处：建立可见的成果让你更擅长实质性法律工作。它迫使你思路清晰，避免专业术语，必须表明立场而非藏身于概括背后。

换句话说，它加速了法学院本该培养的能力。
这些并不取代传统路径。你仍需完成阅读，准备好上课，争取能打开门的资质。
但若仅靠这些，你就错失了机会。

毕业后，你不再只是靠知识竞争。
而是靠别人知不知道你竞争。

因此，是的，这个夏天要读案例。
但也要读懂环境。
想好自己希望被理解的方式，别让职业替你决定。
这或许是法学院第一天前最有价值的准备。

阿曼达·德曼达是阿曼达·德曼达伤害律师事务所创始人，全国知名审判律师，专注于严重和灾难性商业卡车事故诉讼。她现任迈阿密-戴德县审判律师协会会长。在迈阿密、坦帕、休斯敦、达拉斯及佛罗里达州和德克萨斯州各地设有办事处，使其团队能处理主要交通枢纽的高额案件。以结合法庭技巧与战略洞察著称，阿曼达将以人为本、注重安全的理念带入复杂卡车和人身伤害案件，关注责任和现实影响。
articles.summary:
If you’re starting law school this fall, you’ve probably already been told what to read.

Casebooks. Maybe a primer on contracts. Something to get your head around how lawyers think before your first cold call.

That advice isn’t wrong.

It’s just incomplete.

Because your most important summer reading isn’t on your syllabus. It’s everything that teaches you how to be seen and understood as a future lawyer.

That might sound out of place in a profession that still likes to believe that merit speaks for itself. It doesn’t. Not anymore.

By the time you graduate, platforms like LinkedIn and TikTok will play a real role in how employers, clients, and even colleagues encounter your ideas. And tools like ChatGPT are already shaping how legal information is summarized, surfaced, and trusted.

You are not just preparing to practice law.

You are preparing to be interpreted.

Most law students wait too long to think about that.

They focus, understandably, on grades, journals, and internships. Those things matter. But they are not the whole story. The students who stand out today are not just the ones who perform well academically. They are the ones who build a point of view early and make it visible.

That doesn’t mean turning yourself into a content machine. It means becoming legible.

Can someone understand what interests you in the law? Can they see how you think about a problem? Can they find you when they’re looking for insight on an issue that matters to you?

Those are not vanity questions. They are professional ones.

The simplest way to start is also the most uncomfortable. Write something. Not for a class. Not for a grade. For yourself, and for anyone willing to read it.

Take a case you’re following and explain it in plain English. React to a legal development that genuinely interests you. Ask a question publicly that you’re still trying to answer.

Do that consistently, even in small ways, and something important happens.

You stop sounding like a law student.

You start sounding like a lawyer.

There’s another benefit that’s easy to overlook. Building a visible body of work makes you better at the substance of the law. It forces clarity. It pushes you to move beyond jargon. It makes you take positions rather than hide behind summaries.

In other words, it accelerates the exact skills law school is supposed to teach.

None of this replaces the traditional path. You still need to do the reading. You still need to show up prepared. You still need to earn the credentials that open doors.

But if you rely on those things alone, you’re leaving something on the table.

Because when you graduate, you won’t just be competing on what you know.

You’ll be competing on whether anyone knows you.

So yes, read your cases this summer.

But also read the room.

Think about how you want to be understood before the profession decides that for you.

That might be the most valuable preparation you can do before your first day of law school.

Amanda Demanda is the founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers and a nationally recognized trial attorney with a focus on serious and catastrophic commercial truck accident litigation. She currently serves as President of the Miami-Dade Trial Lawyers Association. She has built one of the most visible plaintiff firms in the country, with offices in Miami, Tampa, Houston, Dallas, and throughout Florida and Texas, allowing her team to handle high-stakes cases across key transportation corridors. Known for blending courtroom skill with strategic insight, Amanda brings a people-first, safety-driven approach to complex trucking and personal injury cases, with a focus on accountability and real-world impact.

The post Your Most Important Summer Reading Isn’t On Your Syllabus appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: John Roberts Uses William Howard Taft To Defend His Own Record, Fails
articles.content:
每年，首席大法官约翰·罗伯茨都会撰写一份关于司法系统面临重大问题的简报，并总能每次都搞砸。无论他是在喋喋不休地讨论打字机的历史，还是在编写托马斯·潘恩的虚构作品，这位首席大法官总能提供一份充满空洞思考的圣诞卡式的文字，而世界却在燃烧。

现在他还开了个订阅栏目。

严格来说并非如此。罗伯茨为《追寻》撰写了一篇关于威廉·霍华德·塔夫脱的文章，这是一个关于美国实验"250岁生日"的"复盘"。这篇文章大致回顾了国家从"分裂政府"到"可以派遣海豹突击队第六分队去谋杀你的对手"的旅程。据推测，该项目的策划者请求罗伯茨写一篇关于最能激励他的前任首席大法官的文章，然后惊呆了，因为他提交了一篇关于塔夫脱而不是罗杰·坦尼的稿件。

这篇文章基本上是一篇关于第27任总统兼第10任首席大法官的维基百科式历史。他来自俄亥俄州，曾担任总统，在与西奥多·罗斯福的三方竞争中败北，后来担任了最高法院大法官。这不禁让人想起，保守派法律运动自称相信将其决策根植于历史，但同时展现出对该领域的肤浅理解。罗伯茨花了更多的精力来讨好塔夫脱，而他的助手花了更多的精力试图让他从浴缸里出来。

公平地说，罗伯茨确实提到了塔夫脱在白宫期间的体重增加，以及后来在加入法院之前的减肥。不过，最好的部分被掩埋了。

虽然这篇文章缺乏见解，但它却充满了精彩的评论。《追寻》系列明确要求贡献者保持中立，但他们并没有说不能利用这些文章来宣传自己：

诚然，塔夫特的意见在现代宪法法案书上寥寥无几。一个著名的例外是《迈尔斯诉美国案》，该案支持了总统解除行政部门官员的权力。

六周前，罗伯茨本人在特朗普诉斯劳特案中扩大了总统随意解除的权力——不仅包括行政官员，还包括受法律明确限制的独立机构的官员。当时，罗伯茨称《迈尔斯案》是"里程碑式的判决"，是"我们在这个问题上的最佳词语"。实际上，《迈尔斯案》是当时确立法律的一个激进偏离，这就是为什么几年后它被《汉弗莱的执行人》案推翻了。罗伯茨利用纪念塔夫特的机会，插入了一个宣传点，即他砸掉了联邦治理的承重柱，这一决策仅仅基于一个未能持续十年的判决。

值得注意的是，罗伯茨并没有在文章中利用对《迈尔斯案》的颂扬来解释，为什么它会神奇地将联邦储备局排除在它"关于这个问题的最佳词语"之外。罗伯茨曾尝试解释这一区别，但未能成功，因为他在同一天发布了与斯劳特案和库克案直接矛盾的意见。

讽刺的是，《追寻》项目由科琳·肖根负责，她之所以做这项工作，是因为特朗普在2025年2月解雇了她作为美国档案管理员的职务。这一职位在纸面上没有斯劳特或库克享有的保护，但国会确实在44 U.S.C. § 2103中规定，总统"应当向国会每一院通报任何此类解雇的理由"。只要发一份备忘录给国会就行了。

十八个月后，经过几封专业协会的信件，他仍然没有这样做。

最高法院提升的声望有助于未来的首席大法官挡住对其权威的挑战，例如法院扩充计划和对其里程碑式的民权判决的抵制。

不过，法院扩充计划确实奏效了。"时机转变"法院投降，该法案在完全投降后死亡。至于"对其里程碑式的民权判决的抵制"，这确实描述了法院在1957年与南方州长的斗争。它也非常符合谢尔比县和卡莱斯案。这篇文章希望一些《西翼》爱好者的自由派读者读到它后，认为反对法官接受当事人的奢华度假是站在了布朗的错误一边。我不确定这样的读者是否存在。

塔夫特在体系内运作，只在宪法授权的情况下行动。罗斯福则相反，他认为自己是人民的直接代表，在感受到授权时推进，即使他的行动触及或超越了执行官员在宪法下的权力。

啊。也许泰迪应该将他的行动宣称为"官方行为"，因为听说这自动使其合法。

罗伯茨称赞塔夫特的《民选政府》是"对总统自我约束的辩护，以及对滥用行政力量作为规避宪法设计的手段的批判"。这很难不被理解为对宪法秩序的愿望投射。他和他的同事法官并非同意促进特朗普的滥用——至少他绝望地希望我们这样相信——而是总统需要广泛的、几乎无制约的权力，这样历史才能在他们表现出自我约束时适当地赐予褒奖。

在这篇充满对自己遗产的感情用语的文章中，这可能无意中是最揭示性和令人恐惧的。虽然制定者试图建立机构以防止一个卑鄙的男人夺取帝制总统职位，但罗伯茨则拆除这些防护栏，转而支持某种仪式性的总统禁欲主义。他似乎将美国实验视为一系列总统在英雄旅程中的一个个环节，只有在诱惑达到最大化时才能真正展现他们的道德价值。

有时候这会塑造出一个伟大的政治家。有时候这会让首席大法官坐上屌丝椅。

早些时候：《最高法院屠杀联邦贸易委员会，允许美联储烹饪》
《首席大法官罗伯茨解释为什么托马斯·潘恩实际上喜欢总统豁免权和街头巡逻部队》
《约翰·罗伯茨再次利用司法系统年度报告表达对公众的极大轻视》
《约翰·罗伯茨对公众将最高法院视为"政治行动者"感到震惊，即使他们是政治行动者》
《首席大法官罗伯茨，欢迎来到屌丝椅》
乔·帕特里是《法律之上》的高级编辑，也是"像律师一样思考"的共同主持人。如果您对法律、政治和大量的大学体育新闻感兴趣，可以随时通过电子邮件发送任何提示、问题或评论。您也可以在Twitter或Bluesky上关注他。
articles.summary:
Every year, Chief Justice John Roberts sits down and pens a little newsletter to the nation about the big issues facing the judiciary and manages to blow it every single time. Whether he’s rambling about typewriter history or spinning Thomas Paine fan-fiction, the Chief reliably provides a warmed over Christmas card letter of vapid meditations while the world burns.

Now he’s gone and gotten a Substack.

Well, not exactly. Roberts contributed an essay on William Howard Taft to In Pursuit, a “debrief” of the American experiment on the occasion of its 250th birthday. A mostly rosy look at the national journey from “divided government” to “go ahead and send SEAL Team 6 to murder your rivals.” Presumably, the curators of this project asked Roberts to write about the former chief justice who inspires him most and then scrambled when he turned in a draft about Taft instead of Roger Taney.

The essay is, by and large, a Wikipedia history of the 27th president-cum-10th chief justice. He hailed from Ohio, he was president, he lost in a three-way fight with Teddy Roosevelt, he sat on the Supreme Court. It’s an unintentionally fitting reminder that the conservative legal movement believes in rooting its decisions in history while simultaneously displaying a superficial grasp of the subject. Roberts spends more effort buttering up Taft than staffers did trying to get him out of a bathtub.

In fairness, Roberts alludes to this by mentioning Taft’s White House weight gain, and eventual slimming before joining the Court. Sort of buries the best part though.

But what the essay lacks in insight, it makes up for with pointed remarks. The In Pursuit series explicitly instructed contributors to keep it non-partisan, but they didn’t say anything about using the essays to hype yourself:

To be sure, Taft opinions are few and far between in modern constitutional law casebooks. A notable exception is Myers v. United States, which upheld a President’s power to remove executive branch officials.

Six weeks ago, Roberts personally used Trump v. Slaughter to expand the power of presidents to haphazardly remove — not only executive officials — but officers serving in independent agencies under statutes with explicit checks against removal. At the time, Roberts called Myers a “landmark decision” and “perhaps our best word on the subject.” In reality, Myers was a radical departure from established law at the time, and that’s why it got swatted back by Humphrey’s Executor a few years later. Roberts took the occasion of honoring Taft to slide in a plug for his decision to kick down a load-bearing pillar of federal governance based on a decision that didn’t last a decade.

Of note, Roberts does not use this essay’s lionization of Myers to explain why it would magically exclude the Federal Reserve from its “best word on the subject.” Roberts tried and failed to explain that distinction himself when he issued the directly contradictory Slaughter and Cook opinions on the same day.

Ironically, the In Pursuit project is being quarterbacked by Colleen Shogan, who is only doing this because Trump fired her as Archivist of the United States in February 2025. That role does not have the protections on paper that either Slaughter or Cook enjoyed, but Congress DID see fit to require under 44 U.S.C. § 2103 that the President “shall communicate the reasons for any such removal to each House of the Congress.” Just send Congress a memo. That’s it.

Eighteen months and several professional-association letters later, he still hasn’t.

The enhanced prestige of the Court contributed to the ability of future Chief Justices to stave off challenges to its authority, such as the court packing plan and resistance to its landmark civil rights rulings.

Except, the court packing plan worked. The “switch in time” Court surrendered and the bill died after the capitulation was complete. As for the “resistance to its landmark civil rights rulings,” that does describe the Court’s battle against Southern governors in 1957. It also very much describes Shelby County and Callais. The essay half-hopes some Sorkin-pilled West Wing liberal reads it and decides that objecting to justices taking luxury vacations from litigants puts them on the wrong side of Brown. I’m not sure that person exists.

Taft operated within the system, acting only where he found authorization under the Constitution. Roosevelt, by contrast, saw himself as a direct representative of the people, pushing ahead where he sensed a mandate, even if his actions bumped up against or maybe even beyond the powers of the Executive under the Constitution.

Ah. Perhaps Teddy should have declared his actions as “official acts” because I hear that automatically makes it legal.

Roberts praises Taft’s post-presidency book Popular Government as “a defense of presidential self-restraint and a critique of excessive use of executive muscle as an end run around the Constitutional design.” It’s hard to read this as anything but wishcasting constitutional order. It’s not that he and his fellow traveler jurists agree with facilitating Trump’s abuses — or so he desperately hopes we believe — it’s that presidents require sweeping, nearly unchecked power so history can properly bestow brownie points when they show self-restraint.

In an essay sprinkled with gratuitous references to his own legacy, this unintentionally might be the most telling and frightening. While the Framers sought to build institutions to guard against a venal man capturing an imperial presidency, Roberts knocks those guardrails down in favor of a sort of ritualistic presidential asceticism. Like he envisions the American experiment as a string of presidents on a hero’s journey that only properly reveals their moral worth if the temptations are maximized.

Sometimes that creates a great statesman. Sometimes it lands the Chief Justice in the cuck chair.

articles.title: At This Elite Litigation Boutique, It’s ‘Eat What You Kill’ — And Associates Are Feasting
articles.content:
编辑注：欢迎来到我们的每日栏目《今日金句》。

"我们没有债务，我们的理念是当我们有盈余资本时，会从咖啡师到接待员，从IT人员到法务助理，从律师助理到非合伙人律师，再到合伙人，给所有人发放奖金。我们开发的薪酬体系的核心理念就是'吃你所杀'。"
——威廉·T·里德四世（William T. Reid IV），里德柯林斯律师事务所（Reid Collins & Tsai）创始合伙人之一，在接受彭博社采访时谈及该事务所最近的奖金发放情况。该事务所的律师已经收到最高达17万美元的奖金，里德表示该事务所今年将在四个季度中发放奖金。"我试图创造一个我想年轻时就能加入的事务所，在法庭上站立，亲自做律师该做的工作。"

Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.

We have no debt and we have the philosophy of when we have excess capital we pay everyone, from the barista to the receptionist to the IT guy to the paralegals to the associates to the non-equity partners to the partners. The idea behind the kind of compensation system that we’ve developed is very much eat what you kill.

— William T. Reid IV, senior founding partner of Reid Collins & Tsai, in comments given to Bloomberg, concerning the firm’s recent bonus payouts. Associates at the firm have already received up to $170,000 in bonuses, and Reid says the firm is set offer bonuses in all four quarters this year. “I tried to create the firm that I would have desired to work at as a young lawyer, to get into court, get on my feet, and actually do the work that lawyers do,” he said.
